name: Mobius and Plucker: homogeneous coordinates
summary: Algebraic coordinates made duality and line geometry computational.

name: Axioms for linear (vector) spaces: Moebius, Grassmann, Peano
summary: Directed quantities and weighted points led Grassmann to an abstract calculus of extension, and Peano in 1888 gave the first axioms for a real linear space, soon extended to infinite-dimensional spaces.

name: Jacobi: four squares via elliptic functions
summary: Jacobi derived the four-square theorem from theta functions.

name: Quaternions: non-commutative algebra from the geometry of 3-space
summary: Hamilton's decade-long search for a multiplication on three-dimensional space ended in the four-dimensional non-commutative quaternions, the first prominent non-commutative number system, taken up in physics by Tait.

name: Plucker: line geometry and algebraic curves
summary: Lines became elements of space and numerical characteristics of curves were related.

name: Non-commutative ring theory: Wedderburn structure theory and chain conditions
summary: Quaternions and matrix algebras supplied examples; Wedderburn then classified finite-dimensional algebras into radical and semisimple parts and Artin extended this with chain conditions.

name: Ideals and algebraic number theory
summary: Failure of unique factorisation in rings of integers is repaired by introducing ideal elements, later recast as ideals, which become the central object.

name: Transcendence proofs for e and pi
summary: Liouville, Hermite and Lindemann used analytic constructions to show specific numbers are not algebraic, settling squaring the circle.

name: Matrix algebra as an abstract calculus (Cayley)
summary: Eisenstein and Cayley treated arrays of coefficients as algebraic objects with their own addition, product and inverse; Cayley's memoir gave the first abstract definition and showed quaternions embed as matrices.

name: Transcendental numbers from continued fractions (Liouville)
summary: Liouville used rational approximation by continued fractions to produce the first provably transcendental numbers, then gave an explicit example without them in 1851.
